utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to continue the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am ready, Your Honour, subject only to this, that Mr. Haider has very helpfully asked the technicians to come along because although I'm putting the right stuff in my computer it's not logging so -- but that should catch up with the witness coming in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention one other thing? It's just a tiny point, Your Honour, but we think it is in fact unnecessary for the witness to wear her headphones. She -- as far as we can see she is getting nothing more from the headphones than if she didn't wear them because she can hear -- she can hear in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unless the B/C/S interpreters would want to tell her anything but I don't think that there is a fair chance that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we have in mind to spare her the inconvenience of wearing them all day but if that happens we can alert her very quickly of that, if that were acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm getting ready here, Your Honour. It's all under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We just discussed whether it would bring us anything to ask you to have your earphones on and we finally concluded that it doesn't add anything. So if you would feel better without, then take them off. But nevertheless, may I ask you to wait just a couple of seconds between answer -- question and answer. Ms. Cenic I would also like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Cenic.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am, with respect, going to have to take just a few seconds in a moment to log myself on to get the LiveNote as a result of the technical matter being sorted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Mrs. Cenic yesterday evening were you being asked questions about the municipality administration. After what you described of the peaceable entry into the municipality building and then the move to hotel Park, how many people all together were involved in the administrative running of the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the paper work, just two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you running the municipality in that sense for all the inhabitants of whatever nationality?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Permits to leave Vogosca, to any side, had to be held in order to cross the checkpoints, and that applied to Serbian families as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've talked again about permits but were there other aspects of municipality administration that you were undertaking apart from this matter of the issue of permits?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the supply of fuel was rather restricted so that whatever was available was used for company vehicles, official vehicles. If you can call them that. As well as for the most important uses. Nobody could obtain fuel without something like a voucher or a piece of paper that entitled them to a certain quantity of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were there any other aspects of daily municipal administration that you and your colleague, Branka, undertook?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There appeared a problem of vehicles that had been in the Tas company. Many of them had already been assembled and the looting of those vehicles started, and the thefts, so some of my administrative duties involved an attempt which I'm not saying was a very successful one to channel the few vehicles that were there through a regular procedure which means that pursuant to a decision of the Presidency of the municipality, those vehicles were given to certain people but those people had to have a piece of paper that entitled them to those vehicles, a decision that preceded that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, I'd prefer to come back then to the question of those vehicles at another point, as a discrete topic. Returning to the question of permits for people to travel out of the municipality, more specifically what was the procedure? First of all, a person wishing to leave and pass through these checkpoints, they had to attend personally, did they, at the office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Anybody from the respective family would come to the Park hotel applying for this permit or approval, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that would be signed by somebody, would it, then, the permit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes it would be Ms. Cvijetic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it didn't require to refer it on to anybody else, Mr. Tintor or anybody else, you or Branka could sign?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think you talked about a protocol, you kept a log of -- a book in which you logged these permit issues, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each of these papers had a number which corresponded to the number in the log, and a copy was enclosed in the log as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able to say -- well, you've indicated that it wasn't only Muslims who came for these permits but are you able to give an idea of the number of non-Muslims who came for a permit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number but the ratio would have been -- one-third of Serbs left Vogosca, one-third of Serb families left Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there also any paper work or administration sometimes to be done when a person wanted to leave and obtain a permit in relation to fuel?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, are you asking me whether they obtained fuel to leave? Is that what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Whether there was any additional paper work attached to a question of fuel, petrol, for vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no additional paper work. Either Mr. Tintor or Mr. Koprivica or somebody else from the Presidency or from the municipal administration, I don't know what to call them, asked or instructed us as to what to do. We just did the paper work. How shall I explain that? Since there were no PCs, there was just a typewriter, we simply devised a form. We multiplied it and we filled it out by land.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any procedure or requirement attached to the issue of permits relating to ownership or occupation of property?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me tell you how this happened. People would come to the Park hotel with their ID or any other piece of identifying document. They would give us the name and the family name of the members of the family. We would enter those into our forms and that was that. That is the long and the short of it. If I may put it that way, this was their guarantee that they would be able to go through the checkpoints safely no matter what side they decided to go to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- was there ever any question of anybody being refused a permit?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Never ever was anybody denied that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether, after anybody did leave following obtaining of such a permit, their property was taken over in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody moved into their flats or houses. I really cannot be sure of that. I can't be positive of that. I believe that I'm aware of a few cases involving young men who moved into two or three apartments, and I also know that later on, Serbs arrived from other municipalities and I can only assume that they moved into that property, but I don't know the exact number, nor was it done in an organised manner while I was there. It never occurred to us to do anything of that sort in an organised way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you talked about a few cases involving young men who moved into two or three apartments, you're talking, are you, about young Serb men who moved into apartments that had been vacated by people leaving?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By the time you left Vogosca, which was early July, wasn't it? That's right, isn't it, the date?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date but I would say it was at the end of June or the beginning of July. I know that because for a few weeks, I resided in Trebevic and my family arrived in Trebevic, i.e. in Pale, on the 2nd of August 1992. They arrived from Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. By the time you left, how many Muslims, if you can say, were left in the town of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, I don't know the exact number. I never made an effort to learn the exact number. For a week or two weeks, the number of people who arrived in the Park hotel went up somewhat. I'm trying to calculate how many of them arrived on average a day. I would say that maybe a dozen of them arrived every day on their own behalf, on behalf of their families. Later on this subsided. The numbers were not so great and there were not so many applications. However, since all the paper work has been preserved, I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has had an opportunity to see those documents, but they exist and I think that the most useful thing for you to do would be to have a look at them, to inspect those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that tip, Mrs. Cenic. You're talking about documents, aren't you, that were then taken from Vogosca -- not taken in any sinister way but taken from Vogosca to Pale in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in July 1992. I also asked for those documents to be placed somewhere safe, for safekeeping. I believed that those documents were important and that they were more important for us who were there during those couple of months than for anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they are somewhere safe, they went to Pale, did they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a big box containing the logbook, all the copies, all the paper work. The copies of the papers that had been issued during that period, and that box was first taken to the Kikinda facility and subsequently it was stored somewhere but I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- you said you couldn't say exactly. Are you able to give the Trial Chamber some idea of the proportion of the Muslim population who had left Vogosca by the time you left yourself?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say with certainty is that a few hundred people left. I would not like to go into any speculation in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Leaving aside the overall circumstances, Mrs. Cenic, because I'm not asking you about that, was there any question from what you saw of any Muslims being compelled to leave Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not witness a single attempt or act of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- what you have described by way of municipal administration, it does come to this, doesn't it, that there was certainly by the time you were at the Hotel Park, there was a Serb administration running Vogosca as best it could in the way that you describe, but with a mixed population still of Serbs and Muslims and possibly some Croats, is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population at the time was still mixed, until the end of May, I would say. After that, I believe that a lot of Muslim, i.e. Bosniak, population, left Vogosca. They either went in the direction of Sarajevo or in the direction of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My question was specifically this: That there was -- in a nutshell, there was a Serb administration running Vogosca with a mixed population during those months?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any protest or resistance from the Muslim or for that matter Croat members of the population to that situation where the administration was entirely in the hands of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no protests of any sort. I don't think anybody was able to assemble or get together anywhere in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any attempt or proposal from the Muslim population that they should become involved in the administration that you were conducting?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such attempts. Whether anyone from these particular bodies of authority talked to them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'd like to ask a few questions on a matter which it seems you have dealt with, which are not entirely clear to me yet. You say a few hundred people, talking about Muslims, left. Do you mean families? Do you mean persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, I was referring to the numbers of persons, sir. I have to say that these -- we are talking about are people who are alive and I don't want to speculate. I know for a fact that a few hundred people left in the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand a few people, anything between 200, 400, is that what you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's take the average, then, of 300. What would that mean in terms of proportion? How many Muslims were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know the size of the population in Vogosca. I believe that there were several thousand inhabitants in Vogosca but I believe one ought to look at the statistics. As I've already said, I assumed that the ratio between the Serb and Bosniak population was half-half, 50-50. There weren't many Croats. I already stressed that the Bosniak population was for the most part residing in Vogosca itself, whereas the Serbs owned the landed estates and properties in its environs. But I don't know the exact statistics and numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say approximately 50-50 Serbs, Muslims, approximately. You say several or did you say a few thousand, a few thousand Muslims living there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, there were several thousand inhabitants in all in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a rather small municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Several thousand, 3.000, 2.000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Inhabitants, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I don't know. Perhaps 4.000 to 5.000 inhabitants in Vogosca but it is very difficult for me to give you any number, given that I do not know the statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's start from 4.000 inhabitants in total. That means 50-50 is approximately 2.000 Serbs, 2.000 Muslims. You said one-third of the Serbs moved out, which makes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. If I may be allowed, out of those who applied for a permit guaranteeing them passage past checkpoints, one third of these were Serbs who left Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just -- yes, there could be some confusion because I thought -- one second, please. Yes, there is the confusion because the question was, are you able to say -- well, you've indicated that it wasn't only Muslims who came for these permits but are you able to give an idea of the number of non-Muslims who came for a permit? And then you said, "I can't give you the exact number, but the ratio would have been one-third of Serbs left Vogosca. One-third of Serb families left Vogosca. And now I do understand that it was one-third of those who applied for a permit. Could you tell us how many approximately applied for a permit?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, may I say that I -- until now I have been managing but I am now finding myself hampered by what I'm informed is a technical difficulty, that they have been unable to set up my LiveNote and I was told it could be done in the next break. Normally speaking I would just soldier on but Your Honour once we get into the realm where we are referring back to previous questions on detailed matters like this I am actually really hampered by not having that facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand although I literally read because.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm telling Your Honour I'm hampered. I am. With respect, Your Honour, that's the -- that is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I read to you, Mr. Stewart, all the lines between your question about logging of these permits and your next question about paper work for fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't dispute that, Your Honour, but I'm afraid, with respect, that isn't satisfactory. I'm not blaming Your Honour for this but I must be able to do what Your Honour and everybody else in court can do which is check back through the transcript. And my assertion, Your Honour, which is incontrovertible is that I'm hampered in the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart we will wait until you have your LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but I -- technically whether that now needs a few minutes to be done because we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They came in, as Your Honour saw, and they were unable to do it there and then while I carried on, and I was informed from them through Mr. Josse that the next break would be required. The alternative possibility, Your Honour, is I can move to another computer but I feel more comfortable to know that that was set up and working before I do that. I'm more than happy to do that if that's the more convenient course. I will do whatever is the most convenient thing to ensure that I have that facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, we'll wait for a second until the problems with Mr. Stewart's computer have been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes, I just need to say something to make sure my screen is working. Your Honour, that's working absolutely fine now and I'm grateful to the technicians for sorting that out so quickly. Your Honour, of course, it leaves me without what's happened so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honour was in the course of questions of this witness so perhaps I'll just sit down and then follow my newly established screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Cenic, I'm trying to get an impression on proportions, as a matter of fact. Now you said one-third of those Serbs who applied for a permit left Vogosca. Do you know approximately how many Serbs applied for a permit? Because if these are nine only, then we are talking about three. If we are talking about 300 who applied, we are talking about 100. If we are talking about 900 who applied we are talking about 300. Could you give us an impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stated that I know for a fact that a few hundred Bosniaks left. Now, if we are talking about human beings in terms of numbers, which I believe is a bit painful, and if we said that about 300 Bosniaks left, then I could tell you for a fact that about 100 Serbs must have left in that period of time as well. 100 or more. But at any rate, several dozen Serb families decided to leave Vogosca at that point, and to move wherever. Somebody moved to their relatives' place, somebody went else where. I did not inquire into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, to get the right impression if you say a couple of hundred Muslims left on a total of, as you said, approximately 2.000, that would mean that a majority of Muslims remained in Vogosca S that a correct impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is, Your Honour, what I can tell you with certainty. We are talking about persons who came up and applied for that piece of paper. I cannot vouch for the numbers that left without that piece of paper, and I don't know whether they did leave, in fact, or where they went. That is the part I cannot give you any statement about. I can only tell you what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are talking about paper work which might not reflect reality in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the safest way to go, in my opinion, out of Vogosca, together with one's family and one's belongings in one's own car, because in that particular case, they were not pulled over, they were not stopped. Now, I repeat, whether anyone decided to leave without or outside this particular procedure is something I cannot tell you about or vouch for. There is another matter, and that is that some Serb families left without any piece of paper, they simply started off for Pale or in the direction of Pale without ever returning to Vogosca again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did the same happen to Muslim families.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite possible but I really don't know anything about it and I cannot tell you anything about it really. There was this road heading in the direction of Ilijas, along which a mixed population resided, including Serbs, Bosniaks and Croats, though to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said during your testimony that a rough guess of the total inhabitants of Vogosca was a couple of thousand, 4.000 or 5.000, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was an impression of mine, although I repeat I did not study the statistics of the population in Vogosca and its surroundings. That was my estimation judging by the size of Vogosca itself. I deduced the size of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you are an economist. You know that in science people are talking about ranges of errors. On this 5.000, what would be the range of error looking at your sources? 1.000, 2.000, 3.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my personal estimation, as you put it, as an economist, 1.000 would be allowed as a margin of error because Vogosca is quite scattered, and I mean the environs where there is land and many family houses in town -- in the town itself, there are buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as far as the ratio, Muslims-Serbs, is concerned, you said approximately 50-50. What would be the margin of error you would accept for yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that there would be anything to come under this margin of error. I believe that what I stated was indeed the population of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Chamber received evidence on the 1991 census giving a total population of Vogosca of 20.000, which is four times the number you gave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about its urban nucleus. I cannot vouch for the outlying landed households. I can only tell you about the town proper. The households in the areas around Vogosca all gravitate toward Vogosca. I told you at the start of my evidence, Your Honour, that I lived in Vogosca those two months only in this urban nucleus. That was why I kindly asked that statistics be consulted in this respect. I can only tell you what Vogosca looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although when I asked you about the margin of error for your 5.000 inhabitants you referred to the whole of it. You said a thousand would be allowed as a margin of error because "Vogosca is quite scattered and I mean the environs where there was land the many family houses in the town itself there are buildings." So you included the whole of it. But as far as the ratio, Muslim-Serbs is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, is the witness to be given an opportunity to answer that because that's in effect Your Honour's comment is slightly confrontational, if I may put it that way, in which case the witness should be give and opportunity to answer it, as if it were a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to comment on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stand by what I say. And that is that I really cannot know how many households there are that gravitate toward Vogosca town. I can only talk about the part of Vogosca I lived in and that's the urban nucleus with its streets. As for the villages which come under Vogosca municipality, which as you put it, has 20.000 inhabitants, I don't know anything about them. These are villages that are part of Vogosca municipality. As for Vogosca town, it cannot have more than a few thousand inhabitants. For instance, Sarajevo, the urban Sarajevo is, of course, one thing and the villages gravitating towards Sarajevo are quite a different thing, and their numbers add to the total number of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as the ratio, Muslim-Serbs, is concerned, were you also talking about town only or about the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about Vogosca downtown, the centre of Vogosca, what is Vogosca proper, which means I'm excluding the villages which are practically outside Vogosca, outside of Vogosca itself but do come under its municipality, and in this specific part I'm referring to, I believe that the number of people I told you lived there. As for the households living along the very perimeter of Vogosca, I cannot tell you how many inhabitants lived there but I do know that the land over there was predominantly owned by Serbs, whereas Muslims, as was the case in other Bosnian townships, lived in the town proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that there would be relatively more Muslims in town than there were in the municipality as a whole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding that, again, the ratio was half-half. Of course, I can be disproved by the statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether the relative proportion of Muslims in town would be higher than in the villages around Vogosca town. Because that's what you explained, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite possible. It's quite possible that this half-half ratio, as far as the very centre of town is concerned, tipped in the favour of Bosniaks, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the peaceful takeover of the administration of the municipality, would that cover the whole of the municipality, administratively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How shall I put it? The municipality of Vogosca covered a given territory in administrative terms. Truth to tell, I don't know which villages specifically these were, and I don't know this even today. After the takeover, or rather when the new Presidency was set up, it was supposed to assume the role of the former administrative authorities of Vogosca. However, I don't know to what extent this coincided with the pre-war jurisdiction, since at that stage checkpoints had already been established. Whether the boundaries followed the former administrative municipal boundaries or not, well, I don't even believe that they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This Chamber received evidence that on the totality of Vogosca municipality, that there were 40 per cent more Muslims than Serbs. You just told us that in town, the balance would tip in favour of Muslims, which would mean that at least in town they would be 50, perhaps 60 per cent more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What do you mean that there were 40 per cent more Bosniaks than Serbs? I don't understand that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you have a thousand Serbs, that you have 1400 Muslims. That's 40 per cent more than the number of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the makeup of population in the municipality, in the entire municipality of Vogosca was in terms of percentages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm going to leave this topic myself for the moment. It doesn't mean I wouldn't return to it but, Your Honour, it makes more sense for me to be able to review the whole transcript and return to it, if it's necessary to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mrs. Cenic, who was Boro Radic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Boro Radic was a guy from the streets, as it were, although I don't believe he is one today. At the time, in Vogosca, I heard that he was the leader of some protests mounted in March. I believe he even headed the Patriotic League. It was one of those fierce, rough guys, to put it colloquially.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's take a few points about Mr. Radic. First of all, he isn't one today for the simple reason he's dead, isn't he? He was killed some years ago?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed during the war under rather strange circumstances, so they say, in a battle of some sort but nobody is sure how he actually ended up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- he was a Serb, correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said he even headed the Patriotic League. The Patriotic League, was that a Muslim outfit, a Serb outfit, a mixed outfit, or what?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was some sort of a Muslim, Bosniak organisation, and I really don't know how come that he headed those demonstrations or -- some even say that it was an attempt of a putsch on the eve of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he influential in Vogosca at the time that you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was influential because he had his lad around him, the lads that were loyal to him. He had his own private army, and he was considered a tough guy. I suppose that in every little town you have a situation like that. You have somebody who is practically without education and I really don't know what the origin of his income was. I don't dare comment. I can't tell you what he lived on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, when you say you suppose in every little town you have a situation like that, you're meaning you have a situation with some sort of street-tough guys? You're not suggesting in every little town you have a private army, are you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these tough guys, wherever they can be found, have their own escorts, their own followers, and I believe that everywhere they are treated as a private, little army of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps, and certainly I can take some advantage of your facility with English here, Mrs. Cenic, as you hear my question but are you talking -- your reference to a private army, are you talking more of a street gang or are you talking about something that it would make sense to describe as a -- any kind of army?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] It would be rather street gang which they treat normally as their private army but more like street gang.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you see -- well, thank you for coming to my language for a moment there, Mrs. Cenic. The -- did you see this gang or members of this gang around Vogosca, yourself?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Boro Radic never went anywhere without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of size was his gang?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were at least a dozen of those lads around him at any given time. How many of them were there in total, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they armed at any time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as April, you could see them carrying arms. In the second half of April, as far as I could move around Vogosca, I could see them wearing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we are talking about what sort of weapons, just -- not talking about fine technical details but just a simple description of what sort of weapons.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are mostly pistols of different calibre, what I could see with my own naked eye, I could see pistols of different sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they, this gang of Boro Radic's, during the time you were in Vogosca, did they -- were they ever under anybody's control?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that they were under anybody's control. Some sort of a truce had been arranged between Jovan Tintor and Boro Radic. I heard that the two of them had been in conflict, so for a while there was a truce between the two of them. I really can't say that Boro Radic was under anybody's command or control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Tintor, precision is not important here, Mrs. Cenic, or I don't think the Trial Chamber will regard precision as critical, about how old was Mr. Tintor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Tintor was born in 1951. In any case, between 1950 and 1952.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he -- he was a member of a rather well-off family with property and business interests in Vogosca, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father was a well-respected man. In the Serbian language he was considered a very respected head of family, head of a household. He was a farmer and quite an extraordinary character. They were well-known as a wealthy household in Vogosca and around Vogosca on account of the land that they owned especially Mr. Vlado Tintor, Mr. Jovan Tintor's father. Jovan Tintor himself did not finish any higher schools and as far as I know, he started his career as a decorator, a painter. Later on, he was the owner of a few private companies and was considered amongst the wealthier people in Vogosca according to the then-prevailing standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Radic, what sort of age was he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to say. I believe that at the time, in 1992, he was in his late 30s or early 40s. I really don't know what his age was. He may have been younger, he may have been older as well. He was rather slim, in good physical condition, so it was very difficult to pin the exact age on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He wasn't in his 20s, though?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there -- during the time that you were in Vogosca, was there any type of organised unit of soldiers of any type formed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, during the first weeks of confusion that prevailed, there were no organised units. I at least did not see any units of the former JNA. The first unit, some sort of unit, if you could call it that way, was organised and lined up, which means that men of different ages had gathered, towards the end of April. And this took place in the parking lot in front of the Sonja restaurant. And I can tell you that the scene was rather absurd. It was rather funny, because the way they were dressed was rather ridiculous. They wore whatever they saw fit, and still they were lined up, dressed so colourfully. There may have been 50 of them, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the age range was, as best you can do?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 20 and 50, I'm sure, if I have to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And you said they were organised and lined up. By whom were they organised?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Tintor organised them. He spoke to them at the time. I know that because at that moment I was present at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Jovan Tintor was there, was he, when they lined up?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, although I did not speak to them, I did not ask their name, I did not approach them, I did not introduce myself and I didn't hear their name so as to be able to tell you exactly whether they were all Serbs. But I suppose they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were they -- they or any of them -- armed?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few had rifles. I believe that those were the M-48 rifles that were used in the JNA. I also know their calibre because I had military education at school like we all did, so I was taught how to use the M-48.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Tintor the head or commander of that unit or was somebody else appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that he was the commander of that unit. I believe that later on, that unit was divided into some other units, each of which was headed by somebody else, but I can't give you any of their names because I don't know those names, I don't know what the names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did it, whether it remained a single unit or a divided in the way that you just mentioned, did it remain in existence throughout in some form or another, throughout the time that you were still in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were there for some time but as far as I can remember, a contact was established with the army of Republika Srpska or the army of the Serbian Republic, whatever it was called, so that later on, that unit was reorganised. However, for sometime, for a short period of time, they existed and they were a unit of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say later on that unit was reorganised, how much later on are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that towards the end of May and beginning of June, the army of Republika Srpska sent somebody, I believe that it was Major Josipovic, if my memory serves me well. I believe that he was sent on behalf of the Republika Srpska army and he was in charge of the command in Ilijas and Vogosca. So those units were placed under the command of the army of Republika Srpska, or at least were supposed to be placed under the command of the Republika Srpska army. So the things took a different course and I don't know what happened next after I left Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any -- from -- let's take the time frame from when you moved to the Hotel Park, until you left Vogosca, were there any difficulties about supplies of basic necessities, food and other materials for everyday life in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The biggest problem was water. There was not enough drinking water. As for the food supplies, quite a lot of population there is engaged in farming. It was spring time so there was already some vegetables in the gardens. Jovan Tintor was also a tradesman and he had a lot of supplies of flour and sugar, I believe. He distributed that to the people who did not have any supplies, and my family was like that, because nobody ever thought that they should have big supplies of food. Another problem was the fact that a lot of stores were closed. Some were empty. They had been emptied in one way or another. So it was very difficult to obtain some of the staple foods like oil and similar things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How bad was the drinking water problem?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a huge problem actually. One had to wash themselves. While I was staying at the Park Hotel, we would get water in barrels because the waterworks did not work for some reason and there was no water in the Park Hotel and quite a number of people in Vogosca experienced the same problem so they had to go and drag water from -- from wells, and that's what I remember as one of the major problems. Cigarettes were another problem for smokers. It was very difficult to get hold of cigarettes. It became a problem very early on. Those are the biggest problems that were encountered at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the waterworks -- how far were the waterworks from the very centre of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know whether the problem with the waterworks was that there had been any damage or that people were not turning up for work or some other problem?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only speculate. I was there very briefly and it was 15 years ago. I did not stay there long enough in order to know every manhole, every piece of facility. I don't know where the waterworks was, whether it was on the separation line. I can't speculate. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Cenic. This Trial Chamber does discourage witnesses from speculating so you're absolutely on safe ground there, if you decline to speculate. And I with respect will endorse and follow the Trial Chamber's lead on that. What was -- let's take, as our reference point, the time when you moved to the Hotel Park. What was the expectation among you and your colleagues and Mr. Tintor about how long this crisis, which it clearly was, would be likely to continue?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all convinced that this would be over within the space of a few months and that we would all be able to go back to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any development or formulation that you were aware of any strategy for Vogosca, as opposed to day-to-day managing in the situation you were in?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if there had been a strategy, I never saw it. I wasn't aware of it. Nobody ever told me anything about a strategy. I'll allow myself to say that I am familiar with the mentality of the people there, and if you ask me about a strategy today, I can only laugh. And at that time if somebody told me that there was a strategy I would only be too happy to be aware of that. I personally hoped every day, day in, day out, that this would all come to an end because the atmosphere and the situation was very difficult, a bit strange, undecided, and it was not easy running to and fro and helping my family. And as far as I'm concerned, and as far as the people that I was in touch with were concerned, we waited for all this to end. We would all go home and live happily ever after. And this is all we could think of. If somebody had told me at that time that it would take years for me to go back to my own Sarajevo, I think I would have felt really depressed. I would have been devastated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In May and June 1992, in Vogosca, what was the position so far as personal security and safety of an ordinary person going about their business in the town of Vogosca was concerned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us felt safe, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us, absolutely none of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it as compared, I'm going to make the assumption, Mrs. Cenic, that before all these troubles arose that Vogosca, like any other place, was a place where you could go shopping and go home and expect to be home. So I'm going to start from that base by way of comparison. The -- what -- none of you felt safe. What was the -- what were the real dangers that you felt you faced as you went around Vogosca at that time? What was the worst case that you felt you might face?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that somebody would open fire either from one of the buildings or one of the surrounding hills, which did happen; second of all, when I went to visit my parents and my daughter in Ilijas, fire was opened on the car where I was on several occasions, and it was only my good luck that nothing happened to me. So nobody felt safe. You couldn't go for a walk, for example, and shopping. That was science fiction at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to -- I'm going to come back again in a moment. I'm just going to jump ahead in time with the next question. At some point, Jovan Tintor left Vogosca and went elsewhere; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're referring to. He would leave and he would come back on several occasions, and one of those occasions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll stop you there for a moment. I'm coming back to that but at some point in the summer of 1992 he left Vogosca for practical purposes for good and went somewhere else, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He decided to leave, and he did leave at the beginning of July. He didn't even tell us that he did not intend to come back. He went to Pale. I know that for sure, and I can remember the whole thing very well. He spoke to Dr. Karadzic because he no longer wanted to stay in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he left, did he, as you just described it, it was then a short while before you yourself left Vogosca, was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left and I went up there, and I learned in Pale that he did not intend to go back, and truth be told, the situation in Vogosca by then had changed completely because Boro Radic had gradually taken control over people and particularly over his units, so to speak. On the other hand, Jovan Tintor was always in some sort of conflict with the other members of the municipal administration. I don't know what else to call it. I don't know whether this was still municipality or War Presidency, I can't remember. He was in conflict with Mr. Koprivica and with some other people over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just coming on to another subtopic. It might be a - 10.28 - convenient point for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a convenient moment for a break. But first I would like to ask Madam Usher to escort Mrs. Cenic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break until five minutes to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber would like to share with you some of its thoughts on this morning. The witness testified on movement of population and how she administered the permits to leave. From what the witness told us about her arrival and when the Park Hotel was going to be used, it seems that this happened approximately on from early May 1992, perhaps late April. The Chamber heard some evidence on events which may have caused movements of population in earlier stages in Vogosca and what now the core of the testimony of the witness was that one-third of the Serb families left and that a few hundred Muslims left. That's what we got from her testimony, and I allowed you to finish this subject before you moved to another one. Later on, we learned, and we might have misunderstood that although it was not clear from the language, that was one-third of the Serbs who applied for a permit to leave that left. At the same time, we do not know how many applied. So that leaves us with not much information. Then later on the witness testified that people also would leave without permits, although the witness thought that the safest way to leave with a permit and those leaving without a permit could be both Serbs and Muslims. The witness also told us that whether those obtained a permit left, she couldn't tell us. Finally, the witness showed to have hardly any idea about the population of Vogosca, and even if it should have been clear already on from the beginning that when she referred to the population, inhabitants of Vogosca town itself, then still the information is not in accordance with the 1991 census, because in the 1991 census where Vogosca proper is one out of the 20 areas described in the 1991 census, we still have 10.500 inhabitants, and apart from that, where the witness told us that in town the balance between Serbs and Muslims would be more in favour of Muslims, it's just the other way around because the 1991 census learns us that, whereas in the whole of the municipality, 40 per cent more Muslims than Serbs that in Vogosca town, it was just the other way around, that means 3.700 reported Muslims and 4.700 reported Serbs and even if the category of Yugoslavs which is always a bit of an uncertainty would be included then it certainly was not the case that the balance was more favourable for the town as it was for the whole of the municipality. This learns us at the very end that as far as movement of population is concerned, first of all, we do not know how this relates to perhaps earlier movements of population, April. We heard evidence about that, and I might ask one or two questions to the witness in that respect. But most importantly that we know what two ladies did in an office but what actually happened as movement of population is concerned, we do not know anything at all. That is -- we would like to share with you that our feeling that this information, one-third of the Serb families left and a few hundred Muslims left, that looking at the whole of it, paying proper attention of what the witness knows, what the witness doesn't know, that it is finally information which turns out to be information about what two ladies did in an office, whereas the Chamber really wants to get reliable information, also from the Defence, on what happened as far as movement of population is concerned, and not only on what was seen by two ladies in an office. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, first of all, Your Honour, may I say it is always extremely helpful, and that is extremely helpful, to have such an indication of the Trial Chamber's thinking and the matters that are concerning Your Honours and the areas in which you would appreciate having more information and more evidence. So we certainly with respect, Your Honour, we would heartily encourage Your Honours to do exactly this sort of exercise as often as you feel able to because it is tremendously helpful. Secondly, Your Honour, there is a lot of information in what Your Honour has just said, and in the earlier transcripts and, of course, in the material that has already been put in evidence in this case. As it happens, it's quite clear that this witness will not finish her evidence-in-chief today. Therefore, there is ample opportunity for us on the Defence side to continue work that we have already, of course, put under way and are continuing to try to put together as much material as we can to assist the Court in exactly the areas that Your Honour has just indicated. So therefore, Your Honour, my invitation certainly would be to Your Honours to bear with us on that and for us to leave this topic alone for the rest of the day with this witness because otherwise we are in danger of proceeding on the basis of inadequate material and getting answers which will then simply leave a need to explore further later in the week. But, Your Honour, we bear in mind that. My last comment, and I think it will be my last comment on this is that Your Honour refers to two ladies in an office. But, Your Honour, what the Trial Chamber is seeking has to come necessarily from a number of different witnesses and from a number of different sources, and to characterise two ladies in an office, what I'm primarily doing with this witness is - what I submit is the correct thing to do - I'm primarily asking this witness to tell the Trial Chamber what she knows and she was in Vogosca for a limited period. She wasn't there in April, the beginning of April. If she has no evidence to offer on these matters, then she is not the source of the prospective answers to the questions that are concerning Your Honour. She is a piece of the jigsaw -- no disparagement to her, she is a piece of this very large jigsaw. She is one witness able to tell the Trial Chamber what she knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the Chamber has made these observations in order to find out whether it was -- whether it would assist the Chamber at all to have this specific issue of movement of Muslims and Serbs out of Vogosca municipality to be raised at all with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say there? I will make one further comment with respect. The Trial Chamber, of course, has the ultimate responsibility of delivering judgement in this case subject to any appeal, and therefore, the Trial Chamber knows what it is interested in. The Defence has the task of presenting Mr. Krajisnik's case and so although one hopes there is a considerable overlap, in the course of a witness's evidence-in-chief, it is, Your Honour, with respect primarily for the Defence to make its decisions as to what it wishes to adduce by way of evidence and present to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not challenged. But perhaps the choices made by the Defence in this respect, and I just gave this example as one example, of information that at least in the provisional evaluation of the Chamber did not assist us a great deal. That, of course, in prioritising the subjects to be raised during examination-in-chief, this could play a role and should play a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a question which follows on from that which I know will be of particular interest to Mr. Krajisnik but is also of interest to his Defence team? I apologise if it seems to be a slight digression but it's this, Your Honour: In relation to population movements the Trial Chamber has, and has had for a long time, a report from Dr. Eva Tabeau and a colleague. She does not given oral evidence in this case. I didn't insist that she should or that she was cross-examined. Is the Trial Chamber able to give any indication as to whether it would find expert evidence on the Defence side in relation to population movements of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't give an answer right now on behalf of the Chamber. That's one. But one thing is for sure: The Chamber, as far as movement of population is concerned, is primarily interested on what happened; that is, how many people from where to where, for what reasons, moved and is less interested in small particles of relatively unimportant bureaucratic administration of it. But we'll consider the matter on whether the Chamber would like to have more expertise on the matter. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cenic, Mr. Stewart will continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, I'm asked to ask you if you would go a little bit more slowly for the interpreters. As the recipient of many such requests I'm delighted to be merely the messenger on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, from the time you arrived in Vogosca, were you aware of Mr. Tintor making any trips or visits to Pale before the time that he finally left and didn't return?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I believe it was late April, it may have happened some two to three weeks at the most after my arrival there, Mr. Tintor, with some other people, went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you say who those other people were?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about this. I think it may have been Mr. Koprivica and perhaps someone else with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did Mr. Koprivica have any official position in the municipality or in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he held some position in the municipality before the war. For the duration of my stay there, I believe he was also a member of this Presidency, this crisis Presidency of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at the time of the first visit by Mr. Tintor to Pale, of which you were aware, had a Serb Crisis Staff already been established in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had had some meetings about the organisation of the activity of the municipality in general by that time. I didn't attend these meetings, and I can only give you a hearsay account of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Mrs. Cenic, was -- were the meetings, meetings of what you understood to be a Crisis Staff and to be called a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to me that Sonja Storac or I believe that these meetings sometimes took place in Mr. Koprivica's house as well as in this Sonja Storac house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But was it a Crisis Staff or was it some other body?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was called a Crisis Staff, and it seems to me that later on, it became a crisis Presidency of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Mr. Tintor went to Pale with at least somebody else, on the first occasion that you're aware of, you didn't accompany him, did you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, I didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know who he was going to see, if anybody, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had already heard by that time that something was being set up at Pale, in terms of an administrative body or leadership. I can only tell you that upon their return, they met up with the Presidency and quite possibly with Mr. Krajisnik too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you refer to the Presidency, you're referring there to the Republika Srpska Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what or who did you understand that Presidency to be?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, this duty was assumed by Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, who had been members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This particular duty was performed by the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you said a moment ago in an answer that they had quite possibly met up with Mr. Krajisnik, did you in fact learn from them whether they had or hadn't met Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they had met Mr. Krajisnik too. I don't know whether all of them did or only some of them. Normally the Sarajevo municipalities addressed Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any -- apart from any -- no, I'll rephrase that. Were you aware of any particular connection between Mr. Tintor and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Families Tintor and Krajisnik had been related in terms of Godfathers, one to another. I believe Vlado Tintor was, either in terms of Godfather tore a best man, the interpreter notes, because the term in the B/C/S is the same. With Mr. Krajisnik's parents. At least that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said that you remembered Mr. Koprivica accompanying Mr. Tintor or you thought he had. How were relations between Mr. Tintor and Mr. Koprivica at that time?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this period of time, the only thing I can tell you is that the relations oscillated. They had ups and downs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did they go more up than down from that point on?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In time, the relations between the two of them worsened, but not just between the two of them. Also between Tintor on the one hand and other people in the municipality on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you personally get on well with all these people, Koprivica, Tintor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- or rather, I don't think, I am certain that I had a proper -- correct, proper relationship with the others. The others treated me correctly too. Except for Mr. Tintor, because the relations with him were almost non-existent towards the end. I held his family, especially his mother and father, in high esteem, and I believe that they were the best people from the Tintor family.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- did you learn anything, when Mr. Tintor and Mr. Koprivica or whoever else had been to Pale on that first occasion you mentioned, when they returned, did you learn anything from them about what they had discussed, if anything, with anybody in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they had discussed the establishment of communications. That was the biggest problem at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- for all of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you talk about communications there, do you mean telecommunications, physical road communications, or what?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All forms of communication were a problem in general terms, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- was there any report back to you or any discussion with you on their return from Pale which indicated that there had been discussion in Pale of any sort of military matters?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From that first visit you've mentioned by Mr. Tintor to the point where -- well, when he left Vogosca for good, as you've described, were there further visits of which you were aware by Mr. Tintor to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, he frequently went on his own. I know that. The person whom he saw most often on those occasions -- actually it was Mr. Tintor who insisted on meeting up with Dr. Karadzic. Later on, it became quite clear why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what did become clear?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tintor was looking for a position for himself, and he became Dr. Karadzic's adviser.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say he frequently went on his own. Can you say whether on further occasions during that period he went to Pale with Mr. Koprivica or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they would go separately, as time went on. As far as Mr. Koprivica and others are concerned, I really don't know, and I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever accompany Mr. Tintor on any visit to Pale during this period, May-June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On one or more occasions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was more than once. My sister lived then and still lives in Pale, and I would visit her as well on those occasions. There were a lot of injured people in the Koran hospital that I visited as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was some -- I believe I can lead on this, Your Honours. There was difficulty and risk involved simply in travelling from Vogosca to Pale at this time, was there not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extremely difficult to go from one place to another. At that time, we joked about our journey. We would say that we made clandestine trips there. And I remember on one occasion, this was above the city of Sarajevo, there was a sniper shooter on one of the elevations that opened fire, that opened fire on us, on one occasion, when Mr. Tintor and I travelled in separate cars, because Mr. Tintor liked to have his own security in the car, and it did so happen that there was one occasion when the two of us, who were in the other car, barely managed to survive, although the part of the car, the side of the car where I was sitting, was completely damaged. Those roads or, rather, tracks to Pale were not recommendable, and we knew it, and we often spoke about that. We did not recommend those roads to pregnant women and those who suffered from kidney problems. That's how bad those roads were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you accompanied Mr. Tintor to Pale, did you participate in any sort of business or political meetings that he had?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you learn any more about the content or topics of any meetings or discussions that Mr. Tintor had than you had on the first occasion that you described?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you specifically know the names of anybody that Mr. Tintor did go and see on any of those visits?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he went to see Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, you already mentioned Dr. Karadzic. In addition to Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on other occasions, since Jovan Tintor would never fail to brag that he had met up with Dr. Karadzic, and I can't tell you whether he met up with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Vogosca, did you learn of or become aware at any time of any instructions given from the SDS leadership in Pale in relation to any matters in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you become aware at any time of any such instructions given by anybody in Pale to people in Vogosca in relation to matters in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you had mentioned earlier today, but we didn't pursue the topic, that there were some cars at a -- was it a Tas factory in Vogosca? Is that the name of the factory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was it? Was it a car factory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This factory was where Golf vehicles were assembled, and also there were a number of Audi cars, a few Audis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What, if you can say, what was the total number of cars that had been assembled and were still present there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I have to put it this way: It is difficult to give you a precise number, and I'll tell you why. First of all, when you look from any elevation at the parking lot where those assembled cars were sitting, you would see an endless row of vehicles. And now, why is it difficult to speak about the total number is because in the factory there were still parts that were ready to be assembled. There were also cars that needed to be completed, and I know that later on, those parts were used to assemble new vehicles. That's why I can't give you a precise number. Furthermore, the factory was very difficult to secure and to prevent looting from it. The way the vehicles were stolen and taken away from the company perimeter are just incredible. It is incredible what people's imagination came up with. This was a huge wealth, but also a big curse on Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the location of the factory make the position any more difficult, as far as these cars were concerned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The location of the factory was very close to the separation line. I apologise I'm using the terms that have been devised in the meantime, like, for example, the separation line, because at that time we said that the factory was close to the checkpoint, to the Muslim/Bosniak checkpoint. In other words, the factory was very close to the territory under the control of Bosniaks. Furthermore, that factory was fenced off, but the only thing about -- around it was a wire fence. There was no wall around it. However, if it had been possible to erect a wall around it would still not have been possible to protect the factory from looting. Also it was almost impossible to eliminate the so-called deals that the security people had with some outsiders. For a certain amount of money, those who were on duty in the factory, who were standing guard, would let intruders take vehicles out of the company parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I -- first of all, Mrs. Cenic, can you tell the Trial Chamber, had the factory -- by May 1992, had the factory ceased to be operational in any serious way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before you continue, the Chamber is wondering to hear such a lot of details over the last five minutes on a factory of which, at least to the Chamber it's not yet clear what the importance of these details are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to quarrel with that. Those -- I'm trying to put a stop to that, Your Honour. Those five minutes have already happened and I'm trying to prevent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, these are after five minutes in which the witness told us that although she accompanied Mr. Tintor more than once to Pale, that she couldn't tell us anything more than she did already before, that he would have seen Mr. Karadzic over there. Also it took us five minutes to come to -- we know the family now that, what hospital she visited, patients, we know that the roads were bad, but five minutes just to hear that she doesn't have any information on what seems to be the core of your question is -- that's one's five minutes, now we have got five minutes for the car factory. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I did actually want her to tell the Trial Chamber something about the trial fact -- car factory, Your Honour. That isn't simply an unwelcome adjunct to the questions about Mr. Tintor. But I have Your Honour's point about the need, as far as humanly possible, to discourage examination of extraneous matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, you referred to security -- I'm sorry, I'm just looking for your precise phrase and I'll have to go back a little way. The security people at the factory. Were those private security employees or people connected with the factory?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security could not be provided using the same people that had worked until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So who were they?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the newly established units started standing guard, and also the police were engaged, the police officers from Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. First of all then you're drawing a distinction, are you between the newly established units and the police? That's what you seem to be saying. You're drawing a clear distinction are you there?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you refer to newly established units, first of all, are you at all talking about Boro Radic's people?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about those units that had lined up. I've told you about the unit that was lined up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I wanted to get --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Stewart, may I ask you something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission I'm sure it would be helpful?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me to speak slower and I am speaking slowly but you are interrupting me. Tell me how fast or how slow do you want me to speak?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are two separate points, Mrs. Cenic. It's a perfectly fair observation on your part, if I may say. There are two separate points. You and I probably both need to continue to speak at a pace which is suitable for the interpreters. I'm in the position where I have to strike a balance between, of course, meeting the Trial Chamber's wishes that we avoid extraneous matters; on the other hand I'm also anxious not to interrupt you in the course of your answers.
