Forgive me, everybody, if I occasionally get that balance not perfect for everybody. So what I'm asking you then -- I was just getting Boro Radic's people out of the way, if you like. The security at the factory included Mr. Tintor's group, unit, that you've described, that's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any other unit or group involved in securing the factory apart from Mr. Tintor's people that you've mentioned and the police?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was in June, and there was an attempt to change this and to strengthen the security by involving the military, and the military would have worked in shifts in order to avoid those deals to be clinched and those deals were nothing but bribing the security guards to allow people to enter the factory perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time that you arrived in Vogosca in April, are you able to say what was the ethnic composition of the police in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able from your own knowledge to cast any light or give any information on any changes in the ethnic composition of the police in the time you were in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know whether the police who were participating in the security of the Tas factory were ethnically mixed as a group or not?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the Crisis Staff -- were you able to say whether the Crisis Staff was in day-to-day control of the police in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to that question, I can only say that there was a tension between Tintor and the then-commander of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that his name was Mladen. I can't remember his family name, but he was there before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the nature of those tensions?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A different approach to everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Without too much elaboration, Mrs. Cenic, can you summarise --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One sentence, please? In one sentence. Mr. Tintor wanted and liked to be in control. He wanted to be the utmost boss of things. Of course, not everybody liked that. I didn't like it myself, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your evidence in relation to a number of different people, Mrs. Cenic, appears to be describing Vogosca as a place where a very large number of people were in a situation of tension with a very large number of other people and there was a great deal of in-fighting. Is that an inaccurate summary or is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that they fought amongst each other, although there were such cases between those headed by Boro Radic and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were the --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And opinions that prevailed at the time differed, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've mentioned Boro Radic and his gang. You've mentioned Mr. Tintor and his unit. You've mentioned the police. You've mentioned some involvement of the army from around June. Were there any other significant groups, by which I mean military, paramilitary, armed, organised, were there any other groups of any significance in evidence in Vogosca during May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak of the presence of some paramilitary formations in Vogosca itself. However, those formations existed in other municipalities, such as Ilijas, for example, and sometimes they would enter Vogosca or its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't catch the last bit of interpretation. Oh, I see it is "sometimes they would enter Vogosca." Is that -- is that what you said, Mrs. --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Cenic? Thank you. Did that -- how often did that happen, that other groups from outside entered Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once or maybe twice they entered Vogosca itself. Again, I kindly ask the honourable Chamber to hear me when I say Vogosca itself and what used to belong to the municipality of Vogosca up to 1992 and was treated as municipality of Vogosca, which ceased to be in -- ceased to be the case in the period that I'm talking about. They entered Vogosca itself on one or two occasions, and how often and how frequently they entered the villages around Vogosca, towards Ilijas, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of size groups were they that entered -- when you say Vogosca itself, you mean the town of Vogosca, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What sort of size groups were they that entered the town of Vogosca as you've described?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 or so men. In Vogosca itself, there were no incidents of any nature. They arrived, they spent some time there, an hour or a couple of hours. This happened while we were still at the Park Hotel. And then they left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any -- in May and June 1992, were there any significant outbreaks of violence in the town of Vogosca? And I just want to put on one side sniper fire, significant no doubt, of course, but leaving that to one side, were there any significant outbreaks of violence?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm emphasising the difference. Not in the centre of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How far from the centre of Vogosca did significant outbreaks or outbreak of violence occur in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, several kilometres and more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What were the circumstances, the reasons why you yourself decided to leave Vogosca? What finally caused you to leave?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several reasons. The most overriding one was my family. The old part of Ilijas, as it's called, where my family stayed was also exposed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic I'm here and I hope you understand I obviously don't wish for one moment to minimise the importance of your family which would be central, but we can accept I think that there were family reasons over everything else --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please allow me to finish. What I'm about to say will also illustrate the general situation there. This part of town was also shelled, which caused them to spend most of their time in shelter. The shelling came from the area of Misoca, which was once and is today part of Ilijas municipality. That's why I explained this, because each and every one of these municipalities, even when we spoke in terms of the size of the population, did not find themselves in the same situation in the period up to the month of April and following the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Did you go straight from Vogosca to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a short while, I lived in a house that was not quite completed. It was someone's weekend cottage that hadn't been quite completed up at Trebevic and was later joined by my family. I arrived at the Kikinda facility directly, where there were still offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me just ask you here, Mrs. Cenic, what decided you to go to the Kikinda facility upon your arrival in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So having nowhere to go, why to Kikinda?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I had to do a job of work. Before the war, as I already indicated, I had known both Mr. Krajisnik and Professor Koljevic, including Mrs. Plavsic, Dr. Karadzic and quite a number of people up at Pale, just as I knew Ms. Milena --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's Milena Kusmuk, is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you had wanted to be in Pale to be near to your family and to take care of your family, and also you were needing and wanting some work? Was that your position personally?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several weeks before my family arrived or perhaps a month before they were to arrive, I tried to find out where I was going to put them up and what I was going to do in terms of job. My sister was at Pale also, together with her family. It was only natural for us to reside close to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at that time, in 1992, your English was, for practical purposes, at the same level as it is now, was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. It was a bit poorer because in the meantime, that's to say in the recent years, I had spent some time at Cambridge university attending a post graduate study and my English has improved since, although at that time it was reasonably -- reasonably good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it was at a pretty high level because you had acted as an interpreter and so on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, back then, trying to find a person to interpret for you was quite difficult. Not many people made themselves available or was -- or were willing to do anything. This was especially true for educated people who were seeking to leave the area regardless of their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your first work -- you then started to work, broadly speaking, for Republika Srpska, on your arrival in Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was your first work that you undertook?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a short period of time, I worked in the Ministry of Information, although I must note that I don't recall ever going to that office, not even once. Most of the time I spent working with foreign journalists who were coming to visit at the time. Sometimes I was asked to escort journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you here just to say that at this point in the questioning I'm going to ask you a series of quite short questions to which I would like quite short answers. First of all, where was the Ministry of Information office that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, the offers was at the Hotel Bistrica, up at Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how far was that from the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your work in those first stages, whatever else happened subsequently, your work was mainly done, was it, at the Kikinda building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who else -- I'm not necessarily asking for an utterly exhaustive list down to the people working in the kitchen, if there were, and so on, but who else was working at the Kikinda building at the time that you arrived in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Petko Cancar, Nikola Poplasen also had his office there. There were several people there. Many of them worked there but also spent nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were working for the Minister of Information. Who was the Minister of Information?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did he work up at the Jahorina building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your day-to-day work, and we will come to what that was in a moment, but in your day-to-day work when you were working for the Ministry of information, to whom did you directly report?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially I didn't report to anyone. As I said, literally speaking, I'd be issued with an order or an instruction, if it had to do with journalists. Other than that, I didn't write any reports, nor did any reports exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you expected to work with foreign journalists and domestic journalists or was your work entirely with and for foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there was no job description for what I did, nor were my duties specified. It so happened that in this very short period of time, I dealt with an activity which had to do with a foreign journalist, for a prolonged period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, was that aspect of your work, was that on your own initiative or at somebody else's request?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lady, a Belgrade journalist, Mira Adanja Polak had asked Dr. Karadzic for his assistance. There was a Canadian journalist, George Arthur Kent, who wanted to film a documentary. Dr. Karadzic, knowing that I spoke the language, and not only that, knowing that I was willing to accept any job, he asked me to escort the journalist wherever he wanted to go, which meant to cover with him a better part of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there -- let's stay with Mr. Kent, then, for the moment. Were there particular matters, particular topics, in which Mr. Kent was expressing interest?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it simply, he wanted to see it all. He had no idea whatsoever of the state and of what was actually going on. He had some information that he was able to obtain from other sources, and I don't want to go here into any detail as to the sources, and we simply went on a trip throughout the territory. In this way, we visited the municipalities of Vogosca, Ilijas --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again I'm going to -- please, I hope you don't think it's rude but I'm going to interrupt you because there are questions that are arise before we move on to that. You said Mr. Kent had some information. Did he indicate to you, either directly or indirectly, the nature of that information?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor did I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you even know by way of chapter headings, if you like, what that information related to?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we had already gone into the western part of the country, he sometimes hinted at what it was that he wanted to see, and this included one location that was called collection centre. So we went over there to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I still -- I'm sorry, I still wish to stop you again because there are a couple of preliminary things which are of importance. We are all familiar with journalists not wishing to reveal their sources. You've indicated a reluctance to reveal the journalist's sources here. What -- broadly speaking, the nature of the sources, you said you didn't want to go into detail but you are here in court giving evidence, Mrs. Cenic, what's the nature of the sources of whatever information Mr. Kent had?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you look back at what I said, you'll see that I didn't say that I was hesitant to reveal the sources but rather that I did not ask him about his sources to begin with. I thought that I ought to have shown him whatever he asked for. And I did that. And he saw whatever he wanted to see, without any reservations. What he did with the material he saw is something I am not aware of, although I heard that he was presented with an award at a festival.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just for clarification, then, Mrs. Cenic, when you said -- and for everybody's reference, this is page 41, line 11 of the transcript, what came across in translation, as "I don't want to go here into any detail as to the sources," you --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't want to go into detail. I didn't want to ask about it. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ah. Well, leave it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, this whole trip with this journalist, could you locate that in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to get those preliminary important matters dealt with but the trip itself which is what I now come on to, perhaps, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, did you accompany Mr. Kent on a trip?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the whole trip?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when was it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last week or the last 10 days of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did it go to more than one location?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you able just -- first of all just to list where you went on that trip?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Sarajevo municipalities, including Vogosca, Ilijas and the area there. Then Derventa, Doboj, Brod, the battle at the Obodni Kanal. He saw it all. He interviewed General Lisica. Whatever one was able to see in that period of time, he saw. Of course, Banja Luka and its surroundings too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he was -- was he filming?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it just the two of you on the trip or were you part of a bigger group?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was the man who was both driver and escort, Nebojsa Lazic. When we arrived in Banja Luka, we went to the army's information centre there. We were escorted at Obodni Kanal, at General Lisica's, and at Brod because in the time period we were there, there was fighting. There was fighting for Bosanski Brod or in Bosanski Brod, which ever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you hear that? Perhaps you didn't hear that, Mrs. Cenic. You've been asked by the interpreter if you could repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, therefore, we were joined by another gentleman who was -- whose name was Milos Solaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who was he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the military information centre, or as everyone called it, the military press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kent speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may add, we also toured Prijedor. No, no. I interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you've answered my next question, Mrs. Cenic. So you sat in as interpreter with Mr. Kent on all interviews and discussions he had with Serbian speakers?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all the people he wanted to speak to, which means he spoke to whomever he wanted to, and I interpreted for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- well, clearly, Mrs. Cenic, you must have for the period of the visit have gained a very clear impression of the topics that interested Mr. Kent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what were the main issues which interested him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything specific except for this one matter, which had to do with these collection centres or camps, whichever way they are called, which were the reason why we went to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you went to Prijedor, then, what did you do in relation to that particular issue that interested Mr. Kent?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to see, I believe it was called Trnopolje, and we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how long did you spend there at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could start this next line of questioning now but we are very close to the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for a break. Ms. Cenic, we will have a break for 20 minutes. We'll restart at quarter to one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will reserve the last 15 minutes of this session for procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, 15, I believe is much shorter than 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, when you -- when you got to Trnopolje, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A fence, a gate, many people inside, in conditions that leave the -- left a lot to be desired, a lot of people coming, going, people wearing all sorts of uniforms, a few of them. Some had their heads covered with a hat, some not. In any case, very colourful uniforms, and a lot of people were entering the grounds, even on bicycles. And there were little buildings there that we entered. And as I said, the hygiene conditions there left a lot to be desired. They were rather poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Stop there if I may, Mrs. Cenic, just ask some specific questions again, some short questions, I hope, to encourage short answers. Did you have an appointment so that you were expected at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you got there, did you then approach or contact, ask to contact somebody in charge or did somebody from within the -- Trnopolje take the initiative to make contact with you?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We asked to see somebody that we could talk to. A man approached us, a middle-aged man. As far as I can remember after such a long time, he had a uniform with the trousers and shirt not matching. I explained why we had come, who the gentleman was, and what he wanted. And his idea was to make a documentary, and he was allowed to go on and film the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this middle-aged man was clearly then somebody in a position of some authority?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. I suppose he was in charge of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he did but I can no longer remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he was -- was he an army officer or soldier or was he a civilian or what was he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you then -- you stayed with Mr. Kent, did you, throughout the visit --

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- to this place? And did Mr. Kent more or less immediately begin filming?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He filmed the entrance. He also filmed the pathway leading to the entrance or the road leading to the entrance, because there were a lot of bicycles parked there. He also filmed within the perimeter of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How large an establishment was it? Give some idea by reference to something, please, like football fields or some sort of measure that would give the Trial Chamber an idea of what you remember.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid my memory doesn't serve me too well on such minute details. I believe that it wasn't in the shape of a football pitch. It was more in the form of a circle. I'm talking about the shape of the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was really going by size. I gist wanted to get an idea. Was it as big as 12 football fields or smaller than that?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Smaller than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you -- were you at any point denied access or discouraged from going into any part of the establishment?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you go inside any buildings where people were detained?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, "detained," I don't know how I would describe that situation, because I saw people entering and leaving the grounds. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me put it more specifically then or differently anyway, Mrs. Cenic. Did you see people there in that establishment who were very obviously being kept there, unable to leave, as -- well, we understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask to you find out what happens at this very moment? Are you challenging the adjudicated facts or do you want to establish that matters may have been different in September compared to other periods? It's not entirely clear to me what exercise we are in at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I would like this witness, Your Honour, to tell the Trial Chamber exactly what she observed on the day that she was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you know that adjudicated facts are established on the basis of lots of material and I think it's the case law of this Tribunal that can be challenged, but to add one or two testimonies to the perhaps tens or more on which the adjudicated facts were based is usually not encouraged, because, again, if the Defence wants to challenge and say, in the adjudicated facts, number so and so is not correct and therefore I lead this evidence, then please tell us what adjudicated fact you are challenging through the presentation of this evidence. For example, I could imagine that 365 is there. If that's the case, then at least we know what we are doing at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, 365 what, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Adjudicated fact on our list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour is referring to number 365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes of the adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour that is the advantage of me because I don't have the adjudicated facts in front of me or on my desk. That's why I simply asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you start asking about Trnopolje, we know that as such a list of adjudicated facts on Trnopolje it would be a proper preparation -- exercise to know exactly what is in the adjudicated facts and which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there would be lots and lots of things prior to the proper preparation for witnesses that the Defence could not possibly in a month of somebody's do, but whether or not this is part of it. Your Honour is simply referring to that. If I do not have the list of adjudicated facts in front of me then a simple question for me whether Your Honour was referring to number 365 or a total of 365, I'm afraid I was only asking for that basic help. But, Your Honour, I have to answer Your Honour's question in the absence of the witness since this witness can obviously understand and hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I put it in such a way that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't answer it and accept any answers from the witness, Your Honour. Your Honour's comment can be made in the presence of the witness but if my -- Your Honour has asked me a question which I cannot answer in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I ask myself, Mr. Stewart, I wouldn't mind if you would not turn your back to me at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I was actually -- I've got a co-counsel that I -- that I -- I didn't mean at all to be rude but I have sometimes to have some communication with him without my back to him. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I ask myself what's the use of it at this moment. If you say I'd like to look through the Trnopolje adjudicated facts again, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't answer this in the presence of the witness, Your Honour. If Your Honour is asking yourself questions then Your Honour can answer yourself in the presence of the witness, but I cannot answer Your Honour's question to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few simple questions. Are you at this very moment aware of the adjudicated facts concerning Trnopolje in some detail, yes or no? Because if the answer is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm aware of the adjudicated facts, I'm aware that they go into enormous detail. I'm aware of the nature of them, yes. I am aware of all that, Your Honour. I do not have them here in front of me, but yes, of course, yes, Your Honour, I do know just the sort of thing they deal with. And I do know that they are lengthy and detailed. Well, apart from anything else we know at least that they go to 365, don't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you told us that you would not finish by today. You're invited to first look at the adjudicated facts on Trnopolje before you enter into further details on Trnopolje and the -- just for your guidance Trnopolje goes from 353 up to 371.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we can find all this, Your Honour. I'm grateful for that. Of course, we can find all this, thank you, and I accept Your Honour's offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps at this moment. I'm not saying that the trip as such is excluded from further questions but details on Trnopolje preferably after you have studied --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, still doesn't know and it's not necessary for -- Your Honour still doesn't know the answer to the question Your Honour put to me. So -- which would no doubt have clarified things. But Your Honour therefore I won't, if I understand this fits what the Trial Chamber's preference would be today, I would prefer to leave this topic completely for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, I'm going to go back in time then and take us back to your -- the beginning of your time in Pale. So we are back in Kikinda. The -- I'll lead a bit on this, Your Honour, if I may, and, of course, invite the usual interruptions if I'm going too far. Dr. Karadzic had his own office in Kikinda, did he?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did Mr. Krajisnik? This is at the time you arrived. Did Mr. Krajisnik also have his own office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were Dr. Karadzic's and Mr. Krajisnik's offices opposite, directly opposite each other, on two sides of a corridor?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this right, they were not purpose-built offices but they were nevertheless large rooms functioning as offices; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This used to be a holiday place for the Kikinda and that's why it's called Kikinda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those were just rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who worked, if anybody, in Dr. Karadzic's office as well as him?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His personal assistant, his secretary, worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milijana Rasevic was her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Whoever else went in and out of Dr. Karadzic's office, the two people who were actually based there working were the two of them?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That lady and Dr. Karadzic. And Mr. Krajisnik's office, was it a single, open room or was it divided in any way?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As well as the other office, as you entered, there was a little hallway, a bathroom was on the left. There was a room where the secretary was. And to the right there was a room where Mr. Krajisnik's office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the secretary was who?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Milena Kusmuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you began your work at Kikinda, did you -- were you based in one or other of those offices, Dr. Karadzic's and Mr. Krajisnik's, or somewhere else in the building?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was more familiar with Mrs. Milena Kusmuk, I had my desk there, and in a certain way, I placed myself at the disposal of and I helped her until further notice, until I was told what to do and where to go next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was there -- was there a telephone, both in Mr. Karadzic's office and in Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there internal and external communication from the telephone in Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no internal communication. It didn't exist. Those were regular telephone devices and regular telephone lines. One telephone device was on Mrs. Kusmuk's desk and one was on the desk of Ms. Rasevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a fax machine in Mr. Krajisnik's office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it worked all right for incoming and outgoing faxes, did it?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there a similar machine in Dr. Karadzic's office?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was your -- from when you first started working there, was your day-to-day work exclusively or largely or just in part connected with foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we still didn't discuss work with either foreign or local journalists. They would just spontaneously sometimes approach me. Otherwise, I did all sorts of things, typing documents, and I was just there reflecting on my future and what I would be asked to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you were doing general administrative and PA and secretarial work at that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it's very difficult to use the right words to describe the situation as it was at the time. Given the fact that what we had at our disposal was very primitive in comparison with the then-already-existing technologies. There was a typewriter. There was a fax machine, but the most primitive one. And there was a telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic I'm going to ask a question which gives you a relatively free rein. You would have got a sense of the sort of balance the Trial Chamber is interested in between facts and extraneous, extrinsic detail. But you were there. Nobody else from this -- from this courtroom was there at this time. Please describe, as best you can but as succinctly as you can, a working day for you, how it operated, where you were, what you did, who you saw, what the nature of your work was. Obviously this may take a few minutes but try to give the Trial Chamber a picture of your typical working day at that time.

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would come by in the morning, around half past eight. If Mrs. Kusmuk had other things to do, I would answer her telephone. I would receive fax messages. A lot of people came to the office because there was simply no other way to get in touch but to go there -- to go to places in person. People who came were either ordinary people who had a problem or they were assembly members who arrived from various municipalities, and the working day lasted for as long as there was work. I'm talking about very dire times when we had daily information on casualties, on people who got killed or were injured, and there were a lot of other things that were very hard to deal with. And at any moment somebody had to be there, somebody had to be on duty. We would go to bed very late. I would never leave before nine, ten, or even later. And then I would go to that little house where I slept, which was some ten kilometres away from the place I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you at that time in any sense working for Mr. Krajisnik apart from being in his office physically, but were you working for Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indirectly in some way?

utterances.speaker: SVETLANA CENIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indirectly, to the extent I assisted Ms. Kusmuk, who was his secretary. Also, as I said, people were scarce at the time, and there was no strict division of duties or job description. One had to fall back on one's resourcefulness in dealing with matters and organising them. If I was asked to do something, I would leave my desk and go about it, without asking whose duty that was, in fact, because I seemed -- I felt like I had landed there out of the blue, and that's the sort of atmosphere that reigned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, you said that a lot of assemblymen came to see you and you said that these assemblymen came from various municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... French, transfer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was saying that in your testimony, you stated that where you worked, a lot of assemblymen came to visit you and these assemblymen came from various municipalities, that is what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some municipalities didn't have any other way of communicating other than going there directly, and I remember that this was typical of the Herzegovina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these people invited to come by Mr. Krajisnik or did they come of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no invitations sent. People came out of their own accord, on their own initiative. I never heard of any invitation being sent out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody was always prepared to see them without them having to provide an explanation as to why they had come to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most often, if Mr. Krajisnik was occupied elsewhere, the assemblymen waited in a room which used to be used as a cafeteria on the ground floor and then, when he had time to see them, he would see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ask people to specify why they had come to see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, they didn't even need to say why they were there. They simply showed up and said that they wanted to talk to him, probably talk to us, probably about their problems. They didn't ask much, nor did Ms. Kusmuk ask much. I was never told to ask them what their purpose in coming was. The message we had to relay was that they had to wait until Mr. Krajisnik had time to receive them. Mr. Krajisnik was there. He would spent the entire day there. But, of course, he couldn't throw out of the office whoever was in there to receive them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The next question I have for you runs as follows: How often did these people come? Every day? Were there assembly members who came to see Mr. Krajisnik every day? Just about every day? Or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These weren't just assemblymen. There were ordinary people there as well, to put it that way. I don't know what their position was or if they had any position. They weren't familiar to me, and they didn't seem to be people involved in the public life in general. There were people arriving who were trying to get in touch with their family members or to find out their whereabouts, and they would mostly approach Mr. Krajisnik. There were many people who lost touch with their family members in Sarajevo. In fact, most of the people coming to visit were precisely the ones who had this very grave problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us where these assembly members came from? Could you tell us which municipalities or which areas they came from? I think a while ago you were on the point of giving us details about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I mentioned the Herzegovina municipalities, which were the ones the communication was most difficult with. They went to great lengths to reach Pale. I believe they even had to take the round about way through Serbia. Then there were the municipalities of the so-called Stara Herzegovina. They also had this one option at their disposal. Then there were the municipalities around Pale. Their representatives came sometimes as well. I can't recall at this time whether there were frequent visits from the people from the Krajina municipalities. In fact, I can't recall a single delegation from there. And as I said, all these other people came. I'm telling as far as I can remember. There were many people that went through the building and it's very difficult to remember all their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were these municipality representatives who come from so far afield in such difficult conditions, could you tell us why they were so keen on coming to meet Mr. Krajisnik? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there are several reasons for that. People wanted to know what was to happen next and what they were to do. Most of them and I'm talking about assemblymen and people employed in the municipalities, were eager to hear some words of comfort. This may sound a bit strange to you, but sometimes the effect of the office at Pale was sort of a therapy. They wanted to hear that things and matters were getting resolved and that things were looking up. Very often they would go back home without having solved their problems because it was the sort of time when it wasn't easy to solve problems. Each and every one of them wanted to ask how long the situation was going to last the way it was. And as they were waiting to be received they would chat amongst them and the most prominent question was how long is this going to last?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question: Could one phone from these municipalities, could one phone Mr. Krajisnik from these municipalities, or was this totally impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With some municipalities it was impossible to establish any communication channels including those of telephone lines. Later on the situation somewhat improved but at the time I was there we could not communicate with all the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us at what point in time the lines were up and working again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Telephone lines were operating until sanctions were imposed by Yugoslavia. When we relocated to that other facility which was better fitted for an office, it was the so-called Mali Dom next to hotel Panorama, we had telephone lines that were somewhat different there. Nevertheless the lines operated and quite a lot of the lines was fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were at Kikinda, you said, that most municipalities found it difficult to contact Mr. Krajisnik over the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was difficult. In some cases, there was no telephone communication possible. The only solution left to them was to start off on a trip and go there personally, whoever was able to, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I wanted to spend --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we noticed that, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Cenic, we will finish for the day. Tomorrow we are not sitting. We tried to reschedule but there is a meeting of all judges and therefore we can't sit tomorrow. We would like to see you back next Thursday, the 30th of March at quarter past 2 in the afternoon and then again in Courtroom II. I again instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given and you're still about to give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow Madam Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A few matters. First of all, there is -- that might not have been entirely clear to the parties, I would explicitly admit into evidence the following exhibits: D142, D143, and D148, the details to be found on the list the Registrar keeps. Then P1074, P1075, P1076, P1078, P1080, P1085, P1087, P1093, P1094, P1095, P1096, and P1097. Then, as far as P1138 is concerned, these are the, if I could call them, the Hotic documents, they are numbered as follows, and they are by now included in the list of exhibits kept by the Registrar: P1138 is the index of documents pertaining to the Hotic case, K T-460/04. And then all the underlying documents are numbered P1138.A, P1138.B, et cetera, up to and including P1138.A.A, which is then the 27th document. Translations, as always, with a ".1" added to it. The next issue in order not to lose any time next Thursday is the following, and we should turn into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Josse, there were a few matters you could still deal with as the first one being translation of D106. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon has got copies and I'm grateful to the Prosecution. In short, Your Honour, we came to an agreement. It was sent to the CLSS. Document was translated and Mr. Harmon's translators have added to that translation and I'm very grateful to the Prosecution for assisting in that regard. D106 is now agreed between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's mainly about the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I receive French on the English channel but -- now I hear myself again so that's English at this moment. The -- there was an issue about Poplasen testimony about a double punch in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The position is I've received some translations from my learned friend. That is an issue that I would ask be put over to next week, please. Mr. Krajisnik has done some work on the subject and I'm going to discuss it with him in conference tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll give you time until next week to deal with that matter. Yes. Going back for one second to D106, it was only the translation that caused the problems, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That, as far as I'm concerned, and I see Mr. Harmon nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Agreement on the translation means that the -- D106 is admitted with this new translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May I Your Honour, it's the Japra Valley issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Japra Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am content for Mr. Harmon to inform the Court orally of his investigator's investigation, with this rider, that we continue to make such efforts as we can to supplement any of this information; if we are able to provide anything to the Chamber we will revert in due course. But I'm content for Mr. Harmon to deal with the matter by way of a short, oral statement in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my precise notes are in my office, if I can give a more fulsome description to the court when we next meet but essentially there is the situation. The court had asked a witness if there are any Prosecutions for crimes that were committed in the Japra Valley on the 23rd and the 24th of May 1992. As a result of that, my investigators did conduct an investigation by going to the -- I think it was the Bosanski Novi basic court and made an inquiry. They were given certain files, copies of which I have provided in their entirety to the Defence for their review. There were no prosecutions for crimes that were committed in the Japra Valley on the 23rd and the 24th of May 1992. That's based on a review of the files that we were provided by the basic district court that I've looked at and the Defence have looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, if anything could contradict that in due course, then we will notify my learned friend and in due course notify the Chamber but that's the state of the evidence at the moment, I accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Then looking at the clock it's a quarter to two. We have to finish for the day. One second, please. And before we do so, Mr. Stewart, I listened carefully to what you said when I tried, as friendly as possible, to say that I wouldn't mind if you would not turn your back to me. You explained that you've got co-counsel and that you have to be in communication with him without your back to him. Just as guidance, next time, please ask for a second to consult with co-counsel and I'll be only too glad to give you that moment. We will adjourn until next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that guidance, Your Honour. Does that apply to other counsel as well, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn to quarter past two, next Thursday, Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
